title: Hyperliquid: HYPE Risk Compared with Exchange Tokens
content:
Hyperliquid needs two separate readings: HYPE as a traded asset and Hyperliquid as trading infrastructure. The peer comparison above addresses the first by comparing HYPE with other exchange tokens from the same UTC market date. The protocol checks below address risks that this market score does not measure. This editorial explanation was revised on 2026-11-04; the displayed observations carry their own dates.

| Research question | Evidence to inspect |
| :--- | :--- |
| Is HYPE's score unusual among exchange tokens? | HYPE score versus the exchange-token peer median |
| Which inputs explain the difference? | Four contribution rows, capped at 2.5 points each |
| Is the liquidity claim about the token or the platform? | HYPE volume / market cap; no platform-volume substitution |
| What remains outside the score? | Validator, custody, supply and operational checks |

## Compare HYPE with exchange tokens first

Hyperliquid's documentation describes HYPE staking within HyperCore using delegated proof of stake. Its [staking documentation](https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/hypercore/staking) is the primary source for those mechanics. HYPE therefore has a network role that a category label alone does not convey. Comparing exchange tokens is a useful first cut, but the group is not a set of identical economic or operational exposures.

The table selects other published TokenRadar profiles carrying the Exchange-based Tokens category, excludes HYPE, and requires market inputs from the same UTC date. It uses an equal-weighted median for the score, drawdown and turnover comparisons. The downloadable inventory identifies each included peer. It should be checked before interpreting the result as representative of decentralized exchanges or of a broader industry segment.

A smaller risk score describes these observed inputs under TokenRadar's formula. It is not a security rating for a trading platform or a forecast of HYPE returns. Category membership can mix centralized exchange tokens with protocol tokens. That is a reason to inspect the individual observations and their roles before deciding whether the aggregate answers your research question.

## Follow the contributions, not just the final score

The explanation above identifies the largest difference between HYPE's input contributions and the peer means. Market capitalization, drawdown, turnover and cached price-window volatility each contribute up to 2.5 risk points. Their sum is rounded and bounded between 1 and 10. Peer medians summarize the final observed measures; peer means summarize contributions because those contributions add to the unrounded total.

Capitalization above $10 billion contributes zero points; at $500 million or below it contributes the maximum. Turnover at 10% or above contributes zero, while 1% or below contributes the maximum. Between those endpoints, each contribution changes linearly. These thresholds explain why a larger asset or one with higher reported turnover may receive fewer points under the [published methodology](/about#methodology). They do not measure validator independence or establish a valuation floor.

A lower drawdown contribution means the asset is nearer its own recorded high. That is different from being undervalued. Similarly, strong recent trading activity need not persist when volatility rises. Read the four rows together, then compare the result with the wider [risk distribution](/research#risk-distribution) rather than treating the category ranking as a complete assessment.

## Keep HYPE trading volume separate from platform volume

The volume used here is reported trading in the HYPE token. It is not the notional value of perpetual contracts traded on Hyperliquid, protocol revenue, or cash distributed to token holders. Substituting platform activity for token volume would answer a different question and would break comparability with the other observations.

Turnover is also not executable liquidity. It does not state how much HYPE can be bought or sold at a given spread, on a particular venue, or through a particular route. Check the relevant order book, network, fees and custody arrangements separately. The [liquidity depth guide](/learn/liquidity-depth) explains why a daily aggregate cannot replace those observations.

The volatility contribution uses the retained price window dated above. That window may end before the market snapshot, and different peers may have different historical coverage. The export records those dates so readers can identify the limitation. A newly refreshed market cap does not update a stale price series, and a reproducible score is not proof that every input is recent enough for a particular decision.

## Protocol and supply checks outside this score

The [HIP-1 specification](https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/hyperliquid-improvement-proposals-hips/hip-1-native-token-standard) describes native fungible tokens and identifies HYPE as the unit used for deployment gas costs. That establishes a documented use, not a contractual claim on platform income. Any valuation argument based on fees, burns or distributions requires separate current evidence about the mechanism being claimed.

Staking introduces another distinction. The [staking documentation](https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/hypercore/staking) describes a seven-day queue for transfers from staking to spot. Verify the current rule before relying on immediate access to staked HYPE. This access constraint is not captured by the spot turnover ratio, and it should not be inferred from a lower observed market score.

Check circulating supply against total and maximum supply in the market panel, then investigate primary records for any issuance or unlock claim. A gap between these supply measures does not establish an unlock date. The [FDV guide](/learn/fully-diluted-valuation-fdv) gives the valuation context. Avoid turning an incomplete supply observation into an unsupported event prediction.

## FAQ

**Why compare HYPE with exchange tokens?**

It narrows the initial comparison to a relevant category while exposing its limitations. Check the peer inventory because exchange-related assets can have different business models, rights and network roles.

**Does a lower score mean Hyperliquid is safer to use?**

The score covers observed market inputs for HYPE. It does not audit software, validators, custody arrangements, or operational controls for a platform account.

**Where can I reproduce the result?**

Use the comparison JSON above for peer identities, market dates, historical windows and contributions. The upstream [CoinGecko HYPE record](https://www.coingecko.com/en/coins/hyperliquid) can verify market context, with the expectation that current figures may differ from the retained snapshot.

**What research comes next?**

Use the [exchange token category](/category/exchange-based-tokens) to look up peers, then check [how slippage affects execution](/learn/understanding-slippage) when comparing venues. Record those checks independently of the market score.
